newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court allows claim over corrupt judge.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court allows claim over corrupt judge.

text.p: A unanimous Supreme Court ruled Monday that a convicted murderer in Illinois should be able to show he had been denied a fair, impartial trial because the judge in the case later turned out to be corrupt.

The high court said William Bracy, convicted for a triple murder in Chicago in 1980, was entitled to gather evidence to support his claim that he had been denied the right to a trial before an impartial judge.

Thomas Maloney, a Cook County judge who presided over the case, later was convicted as part of a federal investigation into judicial corruption. Bracy claimed the judge's taking bribes may have influenced decisions in other cases.
He argued that Maloney had an interest in making sure that Bracy was convicted to deflect any suspicion that he was taking bribes in other murder cases around the same time.

Writing for the court, Chief Justice William Rehnquist said the Constitution requires a fair trial before a judge without bias against the defendant or an interest in the outcome of a particular case.
If Bracy proves the judge was biased because he did not want to appear "soft" on criminal defendants, there would be no question his constitutional rights had been violated, he said.
Rehnquist said Bracy had made a sufficient factual showing to pursue his claims, although he added that it remained to be determined if there had been actual judicial bias at the trial.
